extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of journalism (journalism historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical standards for selecting, presenting, and allocating newspaper coverage (what makes a 'big' story, how papers decide placement and duration, and how resources, technology, ethics, and censorship shape reporting). Applicable to evaluating news judgment and newsroom practices in the 1914–1940 period.

rubrics_metrics.name: The "big-play" story (front-page prominence and duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A promising story may be given "a big play"—front-page prominence and extended coverage—often at the expense of other news of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Played for all it is worth when it has strong human elements with drama and suspense; may crowd other matters of more intrinsic value off the front page for days. Factors enabling big play include abundant material (pictures, features), chain-syndicate echoing (one important paper's big play prompts others), and competition in street sales. Anti-pattern: allowing circulation pressures to displace more intrinsically important news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest as a primary news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with 'human interest'—appealing to basic and universal desires and emotions—attract avid reader interest and justify extended coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors defer to reader interest in human elements when making placement decisions. Examples: Floyd Collins rescue drama, Dionne quintuplets resulting in thousands of pages of features. Use of pictures and features multiplies human-interest appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical categories of 'great' news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain story types are repeatedly identified as the 'great' stories of a period: wars, presidential elections, great disasters, sensational crimes, and built-up sports events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories guide editorial prioritization and resource allocation—e.g., world wars and presidential elections drive sustained coverage. Examples across decades (1914–1940) are given to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness, suspense, and immediacy (scoop and continuous updates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid, immediate reporting and the building of national suspense can make a story preeminent (scoops, exhaustive name-lists, running updates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and papers may publish extra runs and many pages (e.g., Lindbergh arrival coverage, printing thousands of draftee names) to satisfy public demand for up-to-the-minute developments. This can require extraordinary logistical effort and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictures and feature material to amplify coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of pictures, features, and large volumes of material makes it practicable to give prolonged, prominent coverage to a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological advances (wirephoto, automatic printers) and photographic daring (war photographers) increased the possibility and impact of big-play stories. Editors exploit visuals to sustain reader interest; insufficient visual material may limit play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource capacity and allocation (personnel, bureaus, wire mileage, expenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper's or news association's ability to cover major events depends on scale: number of correspondents, foreign bureaus, leased-wire mileage, and financial resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: growth of AP and U.P. client lists and leased-wire mileage, hundreds/thousands of men covering wars, and cable tolls running to thousands per day. Resource constraints influence which events are covered, depth of coverage, and reliance on associations or pooled reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association/service style and editorial tone (A.P. vs U.P.)
rubrics_metrics.description: News associations' own practices—such as by-lines, interpretative dispatches, and visual services—influence the liveliness, tone, and reach of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP's adoption of by-lines (1925) marked greater liveliness; U.P.'s vivid interpretative European dispatches enhanced its prestige. Service territories and language reach also shape what papers receive and how stories are framed. Shifts in association agreements (dissolving exchanges with propagandic agencies) affect reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign correspondence access and censorship constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents' freedom to report is shaped by host-country censorship, military controls, and diplomatic limits; these constraints affect accuracy, perspective, and quantity of front-line reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship regimes (British Ministry of Information delays, French military censorship, German expulsions or post-publication censorship) limited direct reporting and sometimes forced reliance on official communiques. Neutral hubs (Amsterdam) and cable/wireless links helped overcome some barriers. Risks include expulsion, denial of readmittance, and distortion by propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazards and practical difficulties of frontline reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting from war zones or remote disasters involves risks to life, health, equipment (freezing camera shutters), and mobility, which affect ability to gather news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: correspondents threatened or expelled, deaths from malaria, journalists killed in accidents, freezing equipment at extreme cold. Such hazards limit duration and depth of on-site coverage and necessitate allocation of support and safety considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity and ethical restraint in reporting (avoidance of revolting detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are expected to exercise judgment about publishing revolting or sensational details; over-publication of gruesome specifics may attract widespread criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: papers that published revolting details of the Hickman sex crime were widely criticized. Ethical restraint is a criterion for responsible journalism; anti-patterns include gratuitous luridness for circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding 'trial by newspaper' and undue influence on legal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Courtroom reporting must avoid creating a 'grand hippodrome' or prejudicing legal processes; recess statements to the press and sensational trial coverage are censured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Hauptmann trial prompted criticism that recess statements of counsel to the press amounted to 'trial by newspaper.' Editors should balance public interest in trials with fairness to judicial process and defendants' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of sensationalism and 'overplaying' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may overplay stories—treating scandal as romance or exaggerating importance to sell copies—which can be criticized as excess and poor editorial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: coverage of King Edward VIII's abdication had elements some considered 'overplayed' by American papers; editors should weigh intrinsic importance against potential sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting spot news into ongoing feature exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial spot news event may be transformed into sustained features and picture-driven coverage if public interest persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Dionne quintuplets moved from a spot item to continent-wide, ongoing features that generated supplies/equipment and thousands of pages of copy. Editors should consider newsworthiness vs exploitation when extending coverage.
